It is located in the scenic heights of Okuchichibu with an elevation surpassing 1,000 meters, stands as one of the distinguished Chichibu Sanja, or the Three Shrines of Chichibu. Renowned for its spiritual ambiance and historical significance, the shrine has gained prominence as a prime "{{ill|Power spot (spirituality)|en|Power spot (spirituality)|lt=power spot}}" within the Kanto region. It attracts a multitude of visitors keen on experiencing its healing energies, delving into the legends of {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|qid=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}}, a celebrated hero in ancient Japanese lore, and venerating Oinusama, a deity symbolized by a wolf. The presence of an 800-year-old sacred tree alongside the shrine's splendid architecture further amplifies its allure.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|date=2018-12-12|title=Mitsumine Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Geopark|url=https://www.chichibu-geo.com/en/geosite/bunka04/|access-date=2024-04-10|website=Chichibu Geopark {{!}}|language=ja}}</ref>

[[File:Mitsumine Shrine - various scenes - Feb 3 2021.webm|thumb|Mitsumine Shrine]]

'''Mitsumine Shrine''' (三峯神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|en|Shinto shrine|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|Chichibu, Saitama|ja|埼玉県秩父市}}. It was formerly classified as a {{ill|Ken-sha|ja|県社|qid=Q90139226}}{{efn|Ken-sha|qid=Q90139226|lt=Ken-sha|1=modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|qq=ja_comment|qid=Q90139226|qq= 近代社格制度}}<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=What is Mitsumine Shrine? |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E4%B8%89%E5%B3%AF%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE-638822#:~:text=%E3%81%BF%E3%81%A4%E3%81%BF%E3%81%AD%E2%80%90%E3%81%98%E3%82%93%E3%81%98%E3%82%83%E3%80%90%E4%B8%89,%E3%81%91%E3%83%BB%E7%81%AB%E9%99%A4%E3%81%91%E3%81%A8%E3%81%97%E3%81%A6%E6%9C%89%E5%90%8D%E3%80%82 |website=Kotobank |access-date=2024-12-29 |language=ja |first=Digital Daijisen, Seisenban |last=Japan National Dictionary, Nihon Daihyakka Zensho, Digital Daijisen Plus |publisher=[[DIGITALIO]]}}</ref> and is currently listed as a {{ill|Beppyo shrine|en|Beppyo shrine|qid=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine}} under the {{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|en|Association of Shinto Shrines|qid=Q908077|lt=Association of Shinto Shrines}}.

Together with {{ill|Chichibu Shrine|en|Chichibu Shrine|qid=Q2963366|lt=Chichibu Shrine}} and {{ill|Hodosan Shrine|ja|宝登山神社}}, it is one of the {{ill|Chichibu Three Shrines|ja|秩父三社|qid=DELETED_QID}}. At the front of the main hall stands a rare {{ill|Mitsutorii|ja|三ツ鳥居|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11354046}}. The shrine worships the {{ill|Wolf|ja|狼|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to オオカミ|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q18498}} as a guardian deity<ref>[https://books.google.co.jp/books?id=GqZeEE136gYC&pg=PA98 ‘Japanese Lion and Komainu Tales’] by Chikago Uesugi, Ebisukōshō Publishing, 2008</ref>, and instead of traditional {{ill|Komainu|en|Komainu|qid=Q20155846|lt=Komainu}} statues, numerous wolf statues are placed throughout the grounds<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mitsumine Shrine's Guardian is the Wolf: The Divine Dog Statues Everywhere on the Grounds |url=https://good-books.co.jp/blog/blogs/1090/ |website=Good Books - Publisher in Chuo-ku, Tokyo |date=2018-06-15 |access-date=2024-12-29 |language=ja}}</ref>.

== History ==

[[File:Mitsumine jinja.jpg|thumb|1938 Map of Mitsumine Shrine Area]]
According to shrine tradition, during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|en|Emperor Keikō|qid=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō}}, {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|qid=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru}} climbed the mountain on his way to {{ill|Usui Pass|en|Usui Pass|qid=Q847860|lt=Usui Pass}} and established the shrine to honor the nation-building efforts of Izanagi and Izanami{{sfn|Shinpen Musashi Fudoki Kō Mitsumine Mountain}}. During Emperor Keikō's inspection of the eastern provinces, he admired the three mountains surrounding the shrine—{{ill|shiroiwayama|ja|白岩山|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11579633}}, {{ill|myouhougatake|ja|妙法ヶ岳|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11446942}}, and {{ill|Mount Kumotori|en|Mount Kumotori|qid=Q1781878|lt=Kumotori Mountain}}—and bestowed the name "Mitsumine Shrine."<ref>[http://www.mitsuminejinja.or.jp/saijin/index.htm Mitsumine Shrine - Deities and Origins]</ref>.

It is said that {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|qid=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja}}, exiled to the {{ill|Izu Ōshima|en|Izu Ōshima|qid=Q1070580|lt=Izu Islands}}, trained on Mitsumine Mountain{{sfn|Shinpen Musashi Fudoki Kō Mitsumine Mountain}}, and that {{ill|Kūkai|en|Kūkai|qid=Q222227|lt=Kūkai}} enshrined a statue of {{ill|Kannon|ja|観音}} at the site.

{{Original research|Some scholars suggest that the establishment of Mitsumine was influenced by the Shugendō traditions of {{ill|Kumano region|en|Kumano region|qid=Q6443450|lt=Kumano}} due to the similarity of place names.|date=December 2024}}. {{Citation needed|For example, "Ōkumotori" and "Kokumotori" exist in Kumano, while Mitsumine's central peak is called "Kumotori Mountain."|date=December 2024}}.

During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, Mitsumine Shrine became a major Shugendō center, attracting warriors and commoners alike. 

More detailed information on rituals, shrine architecture, and related legends can be found in the full article.
== History ==

=== Founding ===
The shrine's origins trace back to the first century, attributed to the founding by Prince {{ill|Yamato Takeru|en|Yamato Takeru|qid=Q461258|lt=Yamato Takeru no Mikoto}}, a son of the legendary twelfth emperor of Japan, Keikō. During an expedition to subdue eastern clans, Prince Yamato was captivated by the beauty of the land from a ridge he ascended. He dedicated the site to the divine Shinto creators of Japan, Izanami and Izanagi, leading to its naming by Emperor Keikō as "Mitsumine," which translates to "three peaks." This name reflects the distinctive summits of Myōhō, Shiraiwa, and Kumotori, visible to the east of the shrine.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Mitsumine Jinja Shrine {{!}} Chichibu Tourism Website {{!}} Chichibu Omotenashi Tourism Organization|url=https://www.chichibu-omotenashi.com/en/guide/spot_11.html|access-date=2024-04-11|website=www.chichibu-omotenashi.com|publisher=[[Agence japonaise du tourisme]]}}</ref>

=== Development and Decline ===
Formal worship at Mitsumine Jinja commenced in the late seventh century with the arrival of {{ill|En no Gyōja|en|En no Gyōja|qid=Q198946|lt=En no Gyōja}}, the founder of [[Shugendō]]—a synthesis of Shinto, Daoism, Buddhism, and mountain asceticism. A significant enhancement occurred roughly a century later when Kūkai, a revered Buddhist monk, installed a statue of the Eleven-Headed Kannon within a newly constructed Buddhist hall adjacent to the shrine.<ref name=":1" />

The shrine experienced a surge in fame and influence during the Kamakura period, supported by yamabushi (mountain ascetics) and donations from prominent samurai patrons. However, it faced decline in 1352 after supporting Nitta Yoshioki in an uprising, leading to punitive measures from the victorious Ashikaga lords.<ref name=":1" />

=== Restoration and Modern Era ===
A pivotal restoration effort was initiated in 1502 by the Shugendō priest Gekkan Dōman, culminating in 1533 when Mitsumine Jinja was designated a regional head temple for the Tendai sect by Emperor Go-Nara. In 1720, the distribution of wolf amulets by priest Nikkō Hōin, inspired by an encounter with wolves seen as a divine omen, further enhanced the shrine's reputation in the Kantō region.<ref name=":1" />

The Meiji Restoration of 1868 led to the shrine's designation as a purely Shinto institution, following the separation of Buddhist and Shinto practices. The twentieth century saw various renovations and additions, including the construction of Kōunkaku lodge and a café, with significant restorations commemorating the shrine's anniversaries in 2002.<ref name=":1" />

== Cultural and Spiritual Significance ==
Mitsumine Shrine is celebrated not only for its breathtaking location and architectural grandeur but also as a center of spiritual enrichment and cultural learning. The shrine's association with ancient legends and practices, such as those of Takeru Yamato and the worship of the wolf deity Oinusama, underscores its role in preserving and disseminating Japan's rich mythological and religious heritage. The ancient sacred tree, revered for its age and symbolic importance, adds to the shrine's mystique, embodying the continuity and deep spiritual roots of the site.<ref name=":0" />

As a recognized power spot, Mitsumine Shrine offers visitors a unique opportunity to connect with Japan's ancient spiritual traditions against the backdrop of the country's natural beauty. Whether drawn by faith, interest in cultural heritage, or the search for peace and healing, visitors to Mitsumine Shrine find themselves immersed in an atmosphere of serenity and profundity.<ref name=":0" />{{Commons|Category:Mitsumine-jinja}}
